extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in history of philosophy and Francis Bacon
extracted.subtask_description: A close critical essay examining Francis Bacon's philosophy: its aims (practical usefulness), method (induction), temperament, and historical significance, with examples and comparisons to earlier schools. The piece evaluates what Bacon achieved and the limits of his claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary end: usefulness / practical benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy's chief end should be the production of useful, practical effects for mankind rather than abstract speculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly stresses Bacon’s declared aim: practical improvements that "lengthen life, mitigate pain, extinguish diseases... increase the fertility of the soil... furnish new arms... light up the night... annihilate distance" and so on. The author contrasts philosophies devoted to everything except this one useful end with Bacon’s system which proclaimed usefulness and progress as its law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-sense orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy should be directed by common sense and sympathy with ordinary human desires (life, health, comfort, honour, security, friendship) rather than abstruse theorizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon's influence is credited to "direction from common sense," "love of the vulgar useful," and openness about popular notions of good and evil. Anti-patterns include cant and illusion; the essay notes Bacon "had no anointing for broken bones, no fine theories de finibus, no arguments to persuade men out of their senses."

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral philosophy as an empirical, practical science
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral philosophy ought to be a practical, experimental science aimed at curing disorders of the mind and testing what modes of education, habits, books, society, imitation, etc., actually produce moral health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon urged moral philosophers "to consider moral science as a practical science" and to "discover what are the actual effects produced on the human character by particular modes of education..." The essay endorses treating ethics like medicine or surgery: empirical study and experiment, not endless casuistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid abstruse speculative controversies
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from becoming embroiled in refined metaphysical or theological disputes that do not advance practical benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon is praised for scarcely engaging in speculative theology (e.g., "Homoousians and Homoiousians") and for a tolerant, charitable spirit. The author suggests such disputations occupy energy without producing useful improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise works over words (philosophy of fruit rather than thorns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy should aim at tangible results (safety-lamps, vaccination, diving-bells) rather than rhetorical consolation or verbal subtilties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: Stoic consolations vs Baconian action — Stoic tells the smallpox is not bad; Baconian vaccinates. Stoic reproaches after shipwreck; Baconian constructs a diving-bell and recovers cargo. The text uses the contrast "philosophy of thorns and the philosophy of fruit, the philosophy of words and the philosophy of works."

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive method: analysis versus common practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon analysed the inductive method carefully, but induction itself is an old, ubiquitous practice; Bacon did not invent induction nor was he the first to analyse it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that induction is performed by clowns, schoolboys, and infants (examples: learning which days to catch trout, infant expecting milk), and that Aristotle earlier recognised the limits of syllogistic reasoning and the need for induction. Bacon’s analysis is accurate but often states what people already do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules alone are insufficient — need patience, sagacity, judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal precepts for induction cannot substitute for the practitioner's patience, attention, sagacity, and judgement; these personal qualities are decisive for sound induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contrasts Franklin (sound results) with Mesmer's followers (unsound inductions) and gives the example of a jocular judge’s 'three-names cause Jacobinism' induction to show that following comparentiae and rejectio naturarum mechanically can produce monstrous absurdities. Precepts are "too general" to produce sagacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ample, representative instances; beware small-n and biased samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Sound induction depends on sufficiently large and representative collections of instances; there is no precise numerical rule but inadequate sample size leads to absurd conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasises that the difference between a sound and unsound induction often lies in the number and representativeness of instances ("the difference is not in the kind of instances, but in the number of instances"). The Jacobinism/three-names example shows how enlarging the sample can refute a spurious induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide motive by focusing on useful ends to improve methodological care
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important service Bacon rendered was to propose useful ends, thereby motivating careful and patient induction; motive influences methodological quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because mechanics sought to mould things, they practiced careful induction; philosophers whose object was merely verbal disputation were content with superficial induction. By making discovery of useful truth the goal, Bacon gave researchers reason to perform induction rigorously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper claims about method’s egalitarian power
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not claim that procedural rules will equalise the intellectual capacities of all practitioners; methods cannot fully substitute for talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon's claim that his method would reduce differences among minds is criticised as extravagant — knowing rules (grammar, logic) does not make everyone write like Dryden or reason like Chillingworth. Historical experience shows the interval between talent and dunce remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assert the dignity and centrality of practical arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy should defend and elevate practical/mechanic arts as worthy of serious intellectual attention because of their large effect on human happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon argued that the neglect of the arts arose from a contemptuous opinion that diminished the 'majesty of the human mind'; he sought to reclaim the arts for higher intellects and to use improvements in the arts as tests of philosophical principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical temperament: combine audacity with sobriety ('much hope, little faith')
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal philosophical temperament is visionary (believe anything may be done) but sceptical of unverified claims (indisposition to believe that anything extraordinary has been done).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay calls Bacon's mind a "singular union of audacity and sobriety," summarised as 'much hope, little faith'. He was simultaneously expansive in aims and rigorous in sceptical scrutiny ('Mammon and the Surly of his friend Ben').

rubrics_metrics.name: Keenness of observation coupled with breadth of comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellent philosophical/creative work requires both fine, minute observation of particulars and an expansive intellect capable of seeing mutual relations across knowledge domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author praises Bacon’s "keenness of observation" and "amplitude of comprehension" (analogy of a tent that folds small but spreads to house armies). Bacon’s strength was knowing the mutual relations of all departments of knowledge rather than technical mastery of any single science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-disputatious, invitational communication style
rubrics_metrics.description: Present ideas calmly and invitationally rather than combatively; allow readers to 'weigh them well: and take them or leave them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon "never engaged in any controversy" in his philosophical works; his mode was not to attack but to enter 'as a guest,' avoiding polemics and thereby gaining admittance into receptive minds.
